FACT SHEET

RECOMMENDATION: "Solar first"
- The battery on its own: "Battery not yet".
- Solar comes first because it looks materially better than the battery: solar's INDICATIVE payback is about 8 years, against the battery's 37.2 years. Solar comes first only where its payback is at most 0.5 of the battery's.
- Battery size assessed: 10 kWh of usable capacity.

THE DECISION RULE
A battery is recommended now only if its payback falls within both the battery's warranty and the years the household expects to stay in its home.
- The battery's payback: 37.2 years.
- Warranty: 10 years. FAILED: the payback is outside it by 27.2 years.
- Expected years in the home: not given on the form, so this limit could not be tested. Effect: would not change the answer: the payback (37.2 years) fails the 10-year warranty on its own, whatever the stay.

HOW THE SAVING AND THE PAYBACK ARE WORKED OUT
annual saving = kWh moved × (value on release − cost to store ÷ efficiency) + demand saving
payback = (installed price − rebate) ÷ annual saving
- kWh the battery moves in a year: 1,574 kWh
- what the battery charged with in a year: 1,749 kWh, of which 0 kWh (0%) was solar surplus that would otherwise have been exported and 1,749 kWh (100%) was imported from the grid
- value on release, the average rate where the battery discharged: 43.78 c/kWh
- cost to store, the average cost of what it charged with (the import rate when charging from the grid, the feed-in tariff forgone when charging from solar): 25.85 c/kWh
- round-trip efficiency: 90%
- cost to store per kWh delivered, after losses (cost to store ÷ efficiency): 28.72 c/kWh
- margin on each kWh moved (value on release − cost per kWh delivered): 15.06 c/kWh
- demand saving: $0
- annual saving: $237
- installed price: $11,390; rebate: $2,584; net outlay: $8,806
- payback: 37.2 years
- What limits the battery's value: demand in the peak window. The most it delivered in a day was 5.7 kWh, against 10 kWh of capacity; it was full on 0 days of the year, with 0 kWh worth serving left unmet.

- Year 1: -$8,569 (the net outlay of $8,806, less the first year's saving of $237)
- Year 2: -$8,332
- Year 3: -$8,095
- Year 4: -$7,858
- Year 5: -$7,621
- Year 6: -$7,384
- Year 7: -$7,147
- Year 8: -$6,910
- Year 9: -$6,673
- Year 10: -$6,436
- Crossover, the first year the position is no longer negative: year 38
- Every year is at today's prices: no growth.

WHAT THE PAYBACK LEAVES OUT (not priced)
- backup power in an outage. The payback counts bill savings only; keeping essentials running in a blackout is not valued.
- independence from retailer price rises. Prices are held at today's rates, so protection from future rises is not valued.
- evening peak relief. Discharging in the evening eases the network's peak; nothing in the household's number pays for that.
- battery wear. Wear decides which kWh are worth moving (2.0 c/kWh) but is not subtracted from the saving.
- outliving the warranty. The payback (37.2 years) runs past the 10-year warranty, so the battery may not last long enough to break even.

WHAT WOULD CHANGE THE ASSESSMENT: each found by re-running the model
- Battery price (installed, before the rebate), now $11,390: at $6,368 the label moves from "Solar first" to "Battery not yet". ADVICE CHANGES: NO. The battery answer is "Battery not yet" on both sides; its payback at $6,368 is 16.0 years, and the warranty is 10 years. Only solar's lead moves. Solar's INDICATIVE payback, about 8 years, is 0.50 of the battery's on both sides; solar comes first only while that is 0.5 or less. The label moves because solar's lead narrows past that cut-off, not because the answer about a battery changes.
- Feed-in tariff: not applicable, because the household has no solar, so it exports nothing.
- Peak rate (c/kWh added to it), now +0.0 c/kWh: no change in the answer anywhere from -10.0 c/kWh to +19.9 c/kWh, the range searched; it stays "Solar first".
- Adding solar (kW of panels), now 0.0 kW: no change in the battery answer with anything up to 10.0 kW, the range searched; it stays "Battery not yet".
- Adding an EV (overnight charging the bills do not contain), now 0 kWh a year: no change in the answer with anything up to 5,000 kWh a year, the range searched; it stays "Solar first".

HOW CERTAIN THIS IS
- The bill splits use into time-of-use windows, so how much falls in each window is billed, not estimated; only the shape within each window is modelled.
- The figures come from one representative year, carried forward at today's prices. A different year's use or prices would give different figures: they are not a forecast.

THE HOUSEHOLD ASKS
Why is the payback so long?

Answer the question briefly, answering only what was asked: at most four sentences and under 100 words.
reply: The battery saves only $237 a year against a net outlay of $8,806 after the $2,584 rebate, which gives a payback of 37.2 years. Because the home has no solar, all 1,749 kWh it charged with came from the grid at an average cost of 25.85 c/kWh, which leaves a margin of only 15.06 c/kWh on each of the 1,574 kWh it moves. There is also no demand saving. Its value is limited further by evening peak demand: the most it delivered in a day was 5.7 kWh against its 10 kWh capacity.
